mi_iron_mountain.blurb: Iron Mountain sits in the Upper Peninsula, close to the Wisconsin line, in country of old mining towns. Bouldering makes up well over half of the climbing, mostly V0 to V3 with a thin tail of harder problems, and the rest is a mix of sport, trad and top-rope lines from about 5.5 to 5.11, with the middle grades best covered. The rock is hard quartzite and granite, and it climbs two ways: smooth and crackless, or blocky with plenty of jugs. Ridges trend east to west and the crags face south. Carney Powerline and Carney Crag hold the most climbs, with Section 18 and Granite Bluff behind them. At Section 18 the cliffs face southwest and are mostly steep quartzite.

ca_beaches.blurb: A handful of Los Angeles and Orange County beaches have boulders or small cliffs worth a visit, and nearly all of the climbing here is bouldering, with only a few trad, top-rope and sport lines. The grades lean easy: lots of V0 and below and a steady run up through V4, with a few harder problems up to about V9. Corona Del Mar is the largest piece. At Pirate's Cove there is a small cliff band and a big cave, with juggy, sharp holds, tall problems and soft sand landings, and most problems are V4 or easier. Palos Verdes Peninsula has seaside boulders around Lunada Bay and Pelican Cove, where tides matter. Laguna Beach adds a few more.

ca_redding_area.blurb: Climbing around Redding in Northern California is a scatter of crags and boulder spots, with the largest cluster of climbs east along Highway 299 toward Burney. Sport routes lead, mostly 5.10 to 5.12 with some easier lines from about 5.6 to 5.9, and there is a solid set of boulder problems from V1 through V8 plus a few trad, top-rope and aid lines. The Burney limestone crag is the main roped venue: sport on solid but dirty limestone, with poison oak nearby, and its Opposite Main Wall stays in shade nearly all day. Mary Fork Boulders adds a couple of dozen problems, and Dry Creek and Clear Creek Gorge are smaller stops.

co_riggs_hill.blurb: Riggs' Hill is a bouldering hill in the Grand Junction area, covered with hundreds of sandstone boulders, and the central section's rock is desert varnished. Almost everything here is a boulder problem, with just a lone trad line. The grades are friendly: V0 is the biggest group, V1 to V3 fill out the middle, and a thinner run of harder problems goes up to about V6. The climbing is split among Riggs' Hill East, Central and West, plus the smaller Escondido Circle. Around the main circular lot in the central section, most of the good boulders lie to the northeast.

il_giant_city_state_park.blurb: Giant City State Park, near Makanda and Carbondale in southern Illinois, has big sandstone bluffs and is known for hard, progressive climbing. Sport routes and boulder problems are about equally common, with a smaller helping of trad. Roped grades run mostly 5.7 to 5.12, with a few 5.13s and some easy leads, and the boulders spread from V1 up to V9 with the weight at V3 and V4. Shelter 1 Bluff is mainly sport and trad. The Devils Standtable Area mixes boulders with rope climbs, and its amphitheater sport lines are steep, bouldery and hard. At Devils Standtable, many bolted lines start with a high first bolt.

nm_palomas_peak.blurb: Palomas Peak is a cliff band on the Sandia massif, reached from the Albuquerque and Placitas side. The rock is limestone with a sharp, textured surface that rewards small edges and smearing. Walls stand about 30 to 70 feet tall, and most climbs are 50 to 60 feet. Sport routes make up most of the climbing, with a good number of trad lines and a couple of top-ropes. Grades run from about 5.7 to 5.14, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.12. The south end is very steep with hard overhanging lines, while the rest is vertical slab with bolts and natural-protection cracks. The sun reaches the cliff late in the morning. Randy's Wall and The Far Side hold the most routes.
